diagnostic_evidence.quote: $t_j-t_{j-1}>\mbox{diam }D_{j-1} /c,\, j=1,2,\cdots,J$. Here $\mbox{diam }D := \sup_{x,y\in D}|x-y|$ denotes the diameter of the domain $D$.
$a(t)\in C([0,T])$ is a real-valued function, and $|a'(t)|<c, t\in [0,T]$.
The time signals excited at different moments can be separated under the Assumption \ref{sump}.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims a rigorous implication of Assumption \ref{sump}(ii) that is false. The arrival window of pulse $j$ observed in far-field direction $\hat{x}$ is $[t_j-c^{-1}\sup(\hat{x}\cdot\Sigma_j),\,t_j-c^{-1}\inf(\hat{x}\cdot\Sigma_j)]$ ($\Sigma_j$ the spatial support at instant $t_j$), so consecutive windows are disjoint only if $t_{j+1}-t_j>c^{-1}(\sup(\hat{x}\cdot\Sigma_{j+1})-\inf(\hat{x}\cdot\Sigma_j))$, a condition involving the displacement $a(t_{j+1})-a(t_j)$, not only diam$(D_j)$. Counterexample: $c=1$, $a(t)=(0.9t,0,0)$, $\Sigma_j$ balls of diameter $2\epsilon$ centered at $a(t_j)$, $t_{j+1}-t_j=3\epsilon>2\epsilon$; Assumption (ii) holds, yet the windows $[0.1t_j-\epsilon,0.1t_j+\epsilon]$ of consecutive pulses overlap because the source approaches the observer at speed $0.9$. The promised derivation ('This can be rigourously derived') is never given; only an example with a receding source is shown. What the paper establishes is only the assumption itself, not the asserted consequence, and the proof of Corollary \ref{cor:added-1} opens by invoking this separability to split measured data into single-pulse far fields.

failure_location.quote: The second assumption ensures that wave signals generated at different instants remain separable due to non-overlapping supports.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen Assumption \ref{sump}(ii) to a displacement-aware, direction-uniform spacing condition (e.g. $t_j-t_{j-1}>(\mathrm{diam}(D_{j-1})+|a(t_j)-a(t_{j-1})|+\mathrm{diam}(D_j))/c$), or restrict the separability claim and Corollary \ref{cor:added-1} to trajectories/spacings for which the arrival windows are provably disjoint.
issues.overall_effect: The data model behind (ISP') — extracting the per-pulse patterns $u_j^\infty$ from recorded time-domain signals — is unjustified for sources moving toward an observation direction at speeds where the diam-spacing no longer separates the compressed arrival windows, and the first step of the proof of Corollary \ref{cor:added-1} rests on the false premise.
issues.title: Assumption (ii) does not ensure separability of signals from different excitation instants
issues.why_classification: The claim is false in a non-degenerate regime (sub-sonic approach motion), so a premise used by Corollary \ref{cor:added-1} must be materially strengthened or its scope weakened; however the fix is local, requires no new proof architecture, and leaves a recognizably comparable result.

Combining \eqref{RIeps}, \eqref{RIf} and \eqref{RIl}, we obtain the range identity

issues.failure_explanation: The statement is false under the stated hypotheses. Counterexample: $c=1$, symmetric band with $\kappa=0$ (the regime explicitly used in Section 5), $D=(0,1)\times\omega$, $S(y)=y_1$ (real, continuous, $|S|>0$ a.e. on $\overline{D}$, vanishing only on one boundary face). Then $\mathcal{T}=M_{S/\sqrt{2\pi}}$ is self-adjoint positive, so $F_\#=F=LM_{S/\sqrt{2\pi}}L^*$, and by the Douglas range-inclusion theorem Range$(F_\#^{1/2})=$Range$(LM_{\sqrt{S}})$. Reducing over slices $s=\hat{x}\cdot y$ (with $\tilde{L}U(\tau)=\int_0^1e^{-i\tau s}U(s)ds$ injective), Range$(L)=\{\tilde{L}W:W\in L^2(0,1)\}$ while Range$(LM_{\sqrt{S}})=\{\tilde{L}(\sqrt{\cdot}V):V\in L^2(0,1)\}$; $W(s)=s^{-1\over 4}\in L^2$ lies in the first but not the second set, so the ranges differ. The cause is that $\mathcal{T}_\#$ (multiplication by $|S|(|\cos(\kappa\cdot)|+|\sin(\kappa\cdot)|)/\sqrt{2\pi}$) is not coercive, so the invoked range identity (Theorem A.1) cannot be applied on $D$. The proof is also independently invalid: operator-norm convergence $\mathcal{F}_\epsilon\to F$ and $\mathcal{L}_\epsilon\to L$ does not imply the range convergences \eqref{RIf}/\eqref{RIl}; the symbol $\lim_{\epsilon\to0}$Range$(\cdot)$ is undefined, the ranges involved are non-closed, and the two 'limits' are taken in different senses (element-wise approximation versus operator norm), so the combination step is a non sequitur.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must either restore the uniform positivity $|S|\ge c_0>0$ of the earlier work (abandoning the advertised generalized source assumption), or establish a corrected range identity for a.e.-positive sources (e.g. involving a range of $LM_{\sqrt{|S|}}$) and rebuild the test-function criterion upon it; the limit-of-ranges argument must be discarded.
issues.overall_effect: The identity \eqref{RI} linking the data operator $F_\#$ to the source operator $L$ — the foundation of the Picard-series criterion and of every indicator function — is unestablished and false as stated for a.e.-positive sources; Lemma \ref{lem4.1}(ii) and Theorems \ref{Th:factorization}, \ref{Th:max}, \ref{Th:kd}, \ref{thm:added-1}, \ref{TH:hull}, \ref{thm:added-2} and Corollary \ref{cor:added-1} lose their proofs.
issues.title: Range identity Range(F_#^{1/2})=Range(L) is false under the relaxed a.e. positivity, and its proof uses an undefined limit of ranges
issues.why_classification: The theorem is false in the advertised regime of sources vanishing on measure-zero sets (explicit counterexample) and its central inference is invalid; every resolution either excludes the advertised regime (major loss of the claimed generalization) or requires a new range identity plus a rebuilt criterion, i.e. essentially new proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then we have $\phi^{(\hat{x})}_{z,\eta} \in $ Range $(L_N)$ for all $N\geq 1$. By Lemma \ref{lem4.1} (ii), it holds that $\phi^{(\hat{x})}_{z,\eta} \in $ Range $(L)$.
By the choice of $y_m$, the set $\{e^{-i\tau a_m}: m\geq 1\}$ is dense in $L^2(0,K)$.

issues.failure_explanation: The biconditional is false: $\phi^{(\hat{x})}_{z,\eta}\notin$Range$(L)$ for every $z,\eta$. If $\phi_{z,\eta}=Lw$ on $(0,K)$ for some $w\in L^2(D)$, then the entire function $G(\tau)=\int_D e^{-i\tau(c^{-1}\hat{x}\cdot y-t_0)}w(y)dy$ coincides with $e^{-i\tau b}$ on $(0,K)$, hence on all of $\mathbb{R}$ by analytic continuation; but Riemann–Lebesgue gives $G(\tau)\to0$ as $|\tau|\to\infty$ (real $\tau$) whereas $|e^{-i\tau b}|=1$. So the 'if' direction fails for every $z\in K_{D,\eta}^{(\hat{x})}$ and, via Picard's criterion, the indicator $I_\eta$ would be $+\infty$ everywhere. The proof is invalid at identifiable steps: (a) the passage from $\phi\in$Range$(L_N)$ (finite spans of pure exponentials) to $\phi\in$Range$(L)$ rests on Lemma \ref{lem4.1}(ii)'s claim Range$(L)=\lim_N$Range$(L_N)$, which is undefined and false in any natural reading — the paper itself states $\{e^{-i\tau a_m}\}$ is dense in $L^2(0,K)$, so the closure of $\bigcup_N$Range$(L_N)$ is $L^2(0,K)\ne$Range$(L)$ ($L$ is compact, hence not surjective), and \eqref{RIfN} is false under this reading; in fact Range$(L_N)\cap$Range$(L)=\{0\}$ by the same analyticity argument. (b) The converse direction treats $\mathcal{F}^{-1}\phi_{z,\eta}$ as $\delta(\cdot-b)$, which is the inverse transform of the full-line exponential, not of $\phi_{z,\eta}\in L^2(0,K)$ (whose zero extension transforms to a sinc-type function); equality $Lw=\phi$ is assumed only on $(0,K)$, so Lemma \ref{supplu} yields no contradiction. (c) The point sequence is chosen depending on the test point ('Choose the set $\{y_m\}$ such that $y=y_1$'), and the norm convergence $F_N\to F$ is asserted for sequences satisfying only (i)–(iii), which enforce no quadrature/uniform-distribution property.

failure_location.quote: For any $\eta \in \R$, there holds $z \in {K}_{D,\eta}^{(\hat{x})}$ if and only if $\phi^{(\hat{x})}_{z,\eta} \in $ Range $(L)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must replace the pointwise test functions by objects that actually lie in Range$(L)$ (e.g. the mollified/integrated test functions of earlier factorization methods) and rederive the strip and moment characterizations as correspondingly weaker (asymptotic or approximate) statements, withdrawing the stated pointwise biconditional.
issues.overall_effect: The central computational criterion — membership of pointwise exponential test functions in Range$(L)$ characterizing the strip, and with opposite directions the excitation instant — is false. The indicator functions $I_\eta$, $W_\eta$, $h^{(\hat{x})}$, $I$ and their discrete analogues have no established discriminating behavior, and Theorems \ref{Th:factorization}, \ref{Th:max}, \ref{Th:kd}, \ref{thm:added-1}, \ref{TH:hull}, \ref{thm:added-2} and Corollary \ref{cor:added-1}, whose proofs repeat these arguments, are invalidated as stated.
issues.title: Pointwise exponential test functions never lie in Range(L): the strip-characterization theorem is false
issues.why_classification: The theorem fails in both directions by an elementary obstruction (analytic continuation plus Riemann–Lebesgue) that no parameter choice avoids; the paper's advertised pointwise test-function criterion must be abandoned or rebuilt with new proof architecture, and all dependent characterization and uniqueness results fail as stated.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In another way,  we may also use the \textcolor{ghx}{SPD} discrete approximation $(F^{(\hat x)})_\#$.

issues.failure_explanation: The stated deduction is a spectral-mapping error. Eigenpairs of $F$ are not eigenpairs of $|\real F|+|\ima F|$ (matrix/operator absolute values): keeping the eigenvectors $\psi_n$ of $F$ and setting $\lambda_n=|\real\tilde\lambda_n|+|\ima\tilde\lambda_n|$ is valid only if $F$ is normal with $\real F$ and $\ima F$ simultaneously diagonalizable. In general these do not commute; in particular the Toeplitz matrix \eqref{matF} is non-Hermitian even for $\kappa=0$ because the row and column grids $\tau_n=n\Delta\omega$ and $s_m=(m-0.5)\Delta\omega$ are offset by half a step (its entries are $F_{nm}=\Delta\omega\,u^\infty(\kappa+(n-m+0.5)\Delta\omega)$, so $F_{nm}\ne\overline{F_{mn}}$). Hence the eigen-data fed into the indicators \eqref{indicator5}–\eqref{indicator7} are not an eigensystem of $(F^{(\hat x)})_\#$, and the computed indicators do not discretize the declared $F_\#$-based criterion.

failure_location.quote: then one deduces that  an eigen-system of the matrix $(F^{(\hat x)})_\#:= |\real (F^{(\hat x)})|+|\ima(F^{(\hat x)})|$ is $\left\{ ( \lambda^{(\hat x)}_n, \psi^{(\hat x)}_n): n=1,2,\cdots,N \right\}$, where $ \lambda^{(\hat x)}_n:=|\real (\tilde \lambda^{(\hat x)}_n)| +|\ima (\tilde \lambda^{( \hat x)}_n)|$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Compute the eigensystem of $(F^{(\hat x)})_\#$ directly (form the matrix absolute values $|\real F|=(F_r^*F_r)^{1/2}$, $|\ima F|=(F_i^*F_i)^{1/2}$, or use the SPD approximation alluded to in the source) instead of transforming the eigenvalues of $F$.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical inversion procedure, as described, computes incorrect spectral data for $F_\#$ whenever $F$ is non-normal (in particular for the half-offset discretization actually used, or any $\kappa\neq0$); the discrete indicators \eqref{indicator5}–\eqref{indicator7} do not implement the stated criterion.
issues.title: Invalid deduction of the eigensystem of F_# from that of F in the numerical algorithm
issues.why_classification: A local linear-algebra error in the algorithm description with a standard direct fix that is even alluded to in the source; no formal result depends specifically on the false shortcut.
